summary: This unit covers the menstrual problems that come from hormones: amenorrhea, anovulation, abnormal bleeding without ovulation, menopause, and early ovarian failure. Exam questions give you FSH, LH, prolactin, TSH, and estradiol and ask you to find where the problem sits, or ask what unopposed estrogen and estrogen loss do to the body.

points: Primary: no menarche by age 15, or by age 13 with no breast development.
Secondary: no menses for 3 months in someone who had regular cycles (6 months if cycles were irregular).
Pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea, so check hCG first.
Breast development shows estrogen has been present; pubic and axillary hair show androgen action.
Hypothalamus: low or normal FSH and LH, low estradiol (low energy availability, heavy exercise, stress, Kallmann syndrome).
Pituitary: low FSH and LH (Sheehan syndrome, pituitary mass); high prolactin suppresses GnRH pulses.
Hypothyroidism raises TRH, which raises prolactin, so check TSH with prolactin.
Ovary: high FSH (and LH) with low estradiol, because estradiol and inhibin no longer give negative feedback.
Outflow tract: normal FSH, LH, and estradiol; no bleed after an estrogen plus progestin challenge.
Asherman syndrome: intrauterine adhesions after dilation and curettage or infection destroy the basal endometrium.
No LH surge or poor follicle development means no corpus luteum and no progesterone.
Causes: PCOS, hyperprolactinemia, thyroid disease, low energy availability; normal near menarche and in perimenopause.
Unopposed estrogen keeps the endometrium proliferating with no secretory change.
The thick, unstable lining outgrows its support and sheds at random: irregular, often heavy bleeding.
Long-term unopposed estrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia and raises endometrial carcinoma risk.
Dysfunctional uterine bleeding is now called AUB-O (ovulatory dysfunction) in the PALM-COEIN system.
Rule out structural causes first: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy or hyperplasia.
Menopause: follicles run out, average age about 51; diagnosed after 12 months without menses.
Loss of estradiol and inhibin removes feedback, so FSH rises most and LH rises too.
Remaining estrogen is mostly estrone made by aromatase in adipose tissue.
Estrogen loss: hot flashes, vaginal and urethral atrophy, bone loss (more osteoclast activity), worse lipid profile and higher cardiovascular risk.
Perimenopause: falling inhibin B lets FSH rise first; cycles become irregular and often anovulatory.
Primary ovarian insufficiency: ovarian failure before age 40 with high FSH and low estradiol.
POI causes: Turner syndrome, FMR1 premutation, autoimmune oophoritis, chemotherapy (alkylating agents), pelvic radiation.
Hirsutism: male-pattern terminal hair only. Virilization adds clitoromegaly, deep voice, temporal balding, and more muscle.
Rapid virilization suggests an androgen-secreting tumor.
Very high testosterone with normal DHEA-S points to the ovary (Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor; PCOS gives milder rises).
Very high DHEA-S points to the adrenal, since DHEA-S comes almost only from the adrenal (adrenal tumor; CAH raises 17-hydroxyprogesterone).
Primary dysmenorrhea: endometrial prostaglandins (PGF2-alpha) at menses cause strong myometrial contractions and ischemia.
Mittelschmerz: one-sided midcycle pain when the follicle ruptures at ovulation.
Infertility types: ovulatory (PCOS, hyperprolactinemia, POI), tubal (scarring after PID), uterine (Asherman syndrome, submucosal leiomyoma).

tricks.label: PALM-COEIN
tricks.text: Structural causes of abnormal uterine bleeding: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy and hyperplasia. Nonstructural: Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified.

tricks.label: FSH follows the ovary
tricks.text: If the ovary has failed, FSH is high. If the brain has failed, FSH is low. If FSH and estradiol are both normal, look at the uterus and vagina.

tricks.label: DHEA-S means adrenal
tricks.text: DHEA-S is made almost only by the adrenal. A very high DHEA-S says adrenal; a very high testosterone with a normal DHEA-S says ovary.

highYield: Secondary amenorrhea: rule out pregnancy first.
High FSH with low estradiol means the ovary is the problem (menopause, POI, Turner syndrome).
Amenorrhea with galactorrhea: check prolactin and TSH.
Amenorrhea after a dilation and curettage with normal hormones: Asherman syndrome.
Anovulation leads to unopposed estrogen, endometrial hyperplasia, and higher endometrial cancer risk.
FSH is the best single lab marker of menopause.
POI is ovarian failure before 40; think Turner syndrome, FMR1 premutation, autoimmunity, chemotherapy, radiation.
Virilization with very high DHEA-S suggests an adrenal tumor; with very high testosterone and normal DHEA-S, an ovarian tumor.
pitfalls: Primary amenorrhea is defined by age 15, or age 13 without breast development; do not wait for 15 when there are no breasts.
Low FSH and LH can come from the hypothalamus or the pituitary; prolactin, imaging, and history separate them.
AUB-O is a diagnosis after structural causes (PALM) are ruled out.
Hirsutism alone is usually PCOS or idiopathic; virilization means much higher androgen levels and needs a search for a tumor.
Primary dysmenorrhea has a normal pelvis; pain from endometriosis or adenomyosis is secondary dysmenorrhea.

dumps.p: Make a table with four rows (hypothalamus, pituitary, ovary, outflow tract). For each, write FSH and LH, estradiol, prolactin if relevant, and two example causes.
l: Pregnancy test comes first for secondary amenorrhea
Hypothalamus: low or normal FSH and LH, low estradiol
Pituitary: low FSH and LH; prolactinoma raises prolactin and suppresses GnRH
Hypothyroidism can raise prolactin through TRH
Ovary: high FSH and LH with low estradiol
Outflow tract: normal hormones
Asherman syndrome is an outflow cause after dilation and curettage
Examples placed correctly (Kallmann, Sheehan, Turner, POI)

dumps.p: Draw two menstrual cycles side by side, one ovulatory and one anovulatory. Show estradiol, LH, and progesterone, and what happens to the endometrium in each.
l: Ovulatory cycle has an LH surge at midcycle
Corpus luteum makes progesterone in the luteal phase
Progesterone turns proliferative endometrium secretory
Falling progesterone causes orderly withdrawal bleeding
Anovulatory cycle has no LH surge and no progesterone
Unopposed estrogen keeps the endometrium proliferating
Lining sheds irregularly and heavily
Long-term risk is endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma

summary: This unit covers inflammation of the male and female reproductive tracts, from local infections like balanitis and candidal vaginitis to ascending pelvic infection and its scars. It also covers endometriosis and adenomyosis, where misplaced endometrium causes cyclic pain and infertility. Exam questions ask for the organism, the tissue finding, or the complication.

points: Balanitis: inflammation of the glans, most often from Candida or bacteria.
Risk: uncircumcised foreskin, poor hygiene, diabetes mellitus.
A tight foreskin traps secretions and favors balanitis; repeated balanitis scars the foreskin and causes acquired phimosis.
Mumps orchitis: after puberty, painful swollen testis days after parotitis; can cause testicular atrophy and reduced fertility.
Epididymo-orchitis in sexually active young men: C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae.
Epididymo-orchitis in older men: E. coli and other gram-negative rods from urinary infection.
Cremasteric reflex is kept in epididymitis, which helps separate it from torsion.
Mucopurulent cervicitis: C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae; friable cervix that bleeds on contact.
Trichomoniasis: punctate hemorrhages (strawberry cervix) with frothy yellow-green discharge.
HSV: ulcerative, necrotic cervicitis, often with painful vulvar vesicles and ulcers.
PID: ascending infection from cervix to endometrium, tubes, and pelvis by C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae, and vaginal flora.
PID findings: cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, fever, purulent cervical discharge.
Salpingitis complications: hydrosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess, tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain.
Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome: perihepatitis with right upper quadrant pain and violin-string adhesions from liver capsule to abdominal wall.
Acute: polymicrobial infection after delivery (especially cesarean), miscarriage, or retained products.
Acute findings: fever, uterine tenderness, foul discharge.
Chronic: plasma cells in the endometrial stroma make the diagnosis; normal endometrium has none.
Chronic causes: retained products, intrauterine device, PID; presents with abnormal bleeding, pain, or infertility.
Endometriosis: endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus.
Theories: retrograde menstruation, coelomic metaplasia, vascular or lymphatic spread (explains distant sites).
Ovary is the most common site; bleeding forms endometriomas (chocolate cysts) full of old blood.
Cyclic bleeding into tissue causes inflammation, fibrosis, and adhesions.
Symptoms: dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, pain with defecation, infertility; uterus is normal in size.
Adenomyosis: endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium.
Adenomyosis gives a uniformly enlarged, soft, tender uterus with dysmenorrhea and heavy bleeding.
Leiomyoma gives an irregular, firm, nodular uterus from smooth muscle tumors.
Candidal vaginitis risk: diabetes, antibiotics, pregnancy, immunosuppression.
Findings: thick white curd-like discharge, vulvar itching and redness, normal vaginal pH (4.5 or less).
KOH preparation shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast.
Lichen sclerosus: thin epidermis with dermal fibrosis forming white, parchment-like vulvar plaques, mostly after menopause.
Lichen sclerosus carries a small increase in vulvar squamous cell carcinoma risk.

C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae (also Trichomonas, HSV)
Ectopic endometrium bleeds with each cycle
Fever, tender uterus; chronic form has plasma cells

charts.title: Endometriosis vs adenomyosis vs leiomyoma
rows: Normal size, may be fixed by adhesions

tricks.label: Adeno-MYO-sis is in the MYOmetrium
tricks.text: The name tells you the site: adenomyosis puts endometrial glands in the muscle wall, so the whole uterus swells and hurts.

tricks.label: Chandelier sign
tricks.text: Cervical motion tenderness in PID is so painful the patient seems to reach for the ceiling light. It tells you infection has spread past the cervix.

tricks.label: Plasma cells mean chronic
tricks.text: Normal endometrium has no plasma cells. Seeing them in the stroma is the marker of chronic endometritis.

highYield: Mucopurulent cervicitis: C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae; strawberry cervix: Trichomonas.
Cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness with fever: PID.
PID followed by right upper quadrant pain: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatitis.
Prior salpingitis raises the risk of ectopic pregnancy and tubal infertility.
Chocolate cyst of the ovary: endometriosis.
Uniformly enlarged, tender uterus with heavy painful periods: adenomyosis.
Curd-like discharge, normal pH, pseudohyphae on KOH: Candida.
White parchment-like vulvar skin in an older woman: lichen sclerosus, with slight vulvar SCC risk.
pitfalls: Endometriosis keeps the uterus normal in size; adenomyosis enlarges it evenly; leiomyoma enlarges it irregularly.
Candidal vaginitis has a normal pH; bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis raise pH above 4.5.
Epididymitis in a young man is usually an STI; in an older man, think E. coli from the urinary tract.
Lichen sclerosus thins the epidermis; lichen simplex chronicus thickens it and does not raise cancer risk.

Spread to endometrium (endometritis)
Spread to fallopian tubes (salpingitis)
Hydrosalpinx or pyosalpinx in the tube
Tubo-ovarian abscess at the tube and ovary
Tubal scarring causes infertility and ectopic pregnancy
Spread along the right paracolic gutter to the liver capsule (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis)
Exam findings: cervical motion and adnexal tenderness, fever

Chocolate cysts and adhesions

Adenomyosis: uniformly enlarged, tender uterus with heavy bleeding

summary: This unit covers reproductive problems present from birth: chromosome disorders (Turner, Klinefelter, fragile X), disorders of sex development, and malformations of the penis, foreskin, uterus, vagina, and hymen. Exam questions test the embryology behind each defect and the hormone pattern that goes with it.

points: Turner syndrome: 45,X or mosaic; ovarian dysgenesis with streak ovaries.
Turner labs: low estradiol with high FSH and LH; presents as primary amenorrhea with no breast development.
Turner findings: short stature (SHOX loss), webbed neck from fetal cystic hygroma, lymphedema of hands and feet.
Turner organs: bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of the aorta, horseshoe kidney.
Klinefelter syndrome: 47,XXY from meiotic nondisjunction.
Seminiferous tubule dysgenesis: low inhibin B, high FSH, azoospermia.
Leydig cell dysfunction: low testosterone, high LH; relatively more estrogen causes gynecomastia.
Klinefelter findings: small firm testes, tall stature with long limbs, gynecomastia, infertility.
X-linked; CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in FMR1.
Full mutation (over 200 repeats) is hypermethylated, which silences FMR1.
Anticipation: repeats expand when passed through the mother.
Findings: intellectual disability, long face, large jaw, large ears, macroorchidism after puberty.
Premutation carriers (about 55 to 200 repeats): women risk primary ovarian insufficiency.
46,XX DSD (old term female pseudohermaphroditism): ovaries with virilized external genitalia.
46,XX DSD causes: 21-hydroxylase deficiency (most common) or excess maternal androgen.
46,XY DSD (old term male pseudohermaphroditism): testes with undervirilized external genitalia.
46,XY DSD causes: androgen insensitivity, 5-alpha-reductase deficiency.
Complete androgen insensitivity: X-linked androgen receptor defect.
CAIS: female external genitalia, blind vaginal pouch, no uterus or tubes (AMH works), undescended testes, sparse pubic hair.
CAIS labs: raised testosterone, estrogen, and LH; breasts develop from aromatized testosterone.
Mullerian agenesis: 46,XX, normal ovaries and pubic hair, absent uterus and upper vagina.
Hypospadias: ventral urethral opening from failed fusion of the urethral folds; linked to cryptorchidism and inguinal hernia.
Epispadias: dorsal opening from abnormal position of the genital tubercle; linked to bladder exstrophy.
Phimosis: foreskin cannot retract over the glans; normal in infancy, or acquired from scarring.
Paraphimosis: retracted foreskin trapped behind the glans, causing edema and ischemia; an emergency.
Cryptorchidism: undescended testis, most often in the inguinal canal; more common in preterm infants.
Higher temperature impairs spermatogenesis; damaged Sertoli cells make less inhibin B, so FSH rises.
Cryptorchidism raises germ cell tumor risk.
Septate uterus: midline septum fails to resorb after the Mullerian ducts fuse; causes recurrent pregnancy loss.
Longitudinal vaginal septum: abnormal fusion or resorption; transverse septum: failed canalization.
Imperforate hymen: hymen fails to perforate; at menarche gives primary amenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, bulging bluish membrane, hematocolpos.

rows: Intellectual disability, long face, large ears and jaw, macroorchidism
Anticipation via mother; premutation causes POI
21-hydroxylase deficiency or maternal androgen (46,XX); androgen insensitivity or 5-alpha-reductase deficiency (46,XY)
Gonads and external genitalia do not match
Salt wasting in CAH; gonadal tumor in undescended testes
Failed septum resorption or abnormal fusion or canalization
Short stature, webbed neck, no breast development
Coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve, horseshoe kidney

charts.title: Primary amenorrhea with a blind vaginal pouch

tricks.label: Hypo is below
tricks.text: Hypospadias opens on the underside (ventral) of the penis. Epispadias opens on top and goes with exstrophy of the bladder (E with E).

tricks.label: Klinefelter labs follow two cell types
tricks.text: Sick Sertoli cells: low inhibin B, high FSH. Sick Leydig cells: low testosterone, high LH. Both gonadotropins rise.

tricks.label: Hair tells the karyotype
tricks.text: Blind vaginal pouch with no pubic hair: androgen insensitivity (46,XY). Blind pouch with normal pubic hair: Mullerian agenesis (46,XX).

highYield: Turner syndrome is the most common chromosomal cause of primary amenorrhea: streak ovaries, high FSH, low estradiol.
Turner: bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, horseshoe kidney, webbed neck, lymphedema.
Klinefelter: small firm testes, gynecomastia, high FSH and LH, low testosterone.
Fragile X: CGG repeat, hypermethylation, macroorchidism, anticipation through the mother.
Hypospadias goes with cryptorchidism and inguinal hernia; epispadias goes with bladder exstrophy.
Cryptorchidism raises germ cell tumor risk and lowers fertility.
Primary amenorrhea with cyclic pain and a bluish bulging membrane: imperforate hymen.
Septate uterus is a classic cause of recurrent pregnancy loss.
pitfalls: Phimosis is a foreskin that will not go back over the glans; paraphimosis is a foreskin stuck behind it.
In CAIS testosterone is high, so the problem is the receptor; in 5-alpha-reductase deficiency testosterone is normal and DHT is low.
Both CAIS and Mullerian agenesis have breasts and a blind pouch; pubic hair and karyotype separate them.
Imperforate hymen has normal hormones and normal breasts; the block is mechanical.

dumps.p: Make a two-column table comparing Turner syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome. Include karyotype, gonad problem, FSH, LH, sex steroid level, body findings, and associated organ problems.
l: Turner is 45,X or mosaic; Klinefelter is 47,XXY
Turner has streak ovaries; Klinefelter has small firm testes
Both have high FSH and LH
Turner has low estradiol; Klinefelter has low testosterone
Turner: short stature from SHOX loss; Klinefelter: tall with long limbs
Turner: webbed neck, lymphedema, bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, horseshoe kidney
Klinefelter: gynecomastia and infertility

dumps.p: Draw the Mullerian ducts fusing to form the uterus and upper vagina. Mark where a septate uterus, a vaginal septum, and an imperforate hymen come from. Then draw the male urethral folds and genital tubercle and mark hypospadias and epispadias.
l: Paired Mullerian ducts fuse in the midline
Midline septum normally resorbs; failure gives a septate uterus
Septate uterus causes recurrent pregnancy loss
Transverse vaginal septum comes from failed canalization
Imperforate hymen traps menstrual blood (hematocolpos)
Failed urethral fold fusion gives ventral hypospadias
Abnormal genital tubercle position gives dorsal epispadias
Epispadias goes with bladder exstrophy

summary: This unit covers benign problems of the penis and scrotum: erectile dysfunction, scrotal fluid and blood collections, varicocele, torsion, priapism, and Peyronie disease, plus the causes of male infertility. Exam questions turn on a few bedside clues: transillumination, position relative to the testis, the cremasteric reflex, and change with standing.

points: Erection needs parasympathetic input (pelvic splanchnic nerves, S2 to S4), nitric oxide, cGMP, and smooth muscle relaxation.
Vascular: atherosclerosis limits arterial inflow; often an early sign of coronary disease.
Neurogenic: diabetes, spinal cord injury, pelvic surgery such as prostatectomy.
Endocrine: hypogonadism, hyperprolactinemia.
Drug-induced (for example some antihypertensives and antidepressants) or psychogenic.
Preserved nocturnal or morning erections mean the nerves and vessels work, which points to a psychogenic cause.
Hydrocele: fluid within the tunica vaginalis around the testis; smooth and transilluminates.
Communicating hydrocele: patent processus vaginalis lets peritoneal fluid in; size changes during the day.
Noncommunicating hydrocele: from infection, trauma, or tumor (also idiopathic in adults).
Hematocele: blood in the tunica vaginalis after trauma, torsion, or tumor; does not transilluminate.
Spermatocele: cystic dilation of the epididymis holding sperm; transilluminates and sits separate from the testis, usually above it.
Simple epididymal cyst feels the same but holds clear fluid without sperm.
Varicocele: dilated pampiniform plexus, a bag of worms that grows on standing and does not transilluminate.
Left varicocele is more common because the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein.
A new left varicocele in an older man suggests renal cell carcinoma blocking the left renal vein.
Testicular torsion: spermatic cord twists, usually from a bell-clapper deformity.
Venous outflow is blocked first, then arterial inflow, leading to hemorrhagic infarction.
Torsion: sudden severe pain, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex; an emergency.
Priapism: painful erection lasting over 4 hours.
Ischemic priapism: sickle cell disease and drugs; trapped hypoxic blood causes cavernosal fibrosis and later erectile dysfunction.
Peyronie disease: fibrous plaque of the tunica albuginea causing penile curvature and painful erection.
Pretesticular: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (low FSH and LH), such as Kallmann syndrome, pituitary disease, or anabolic steroid use.
Testicular: Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, varicocele, mumps orchitis; FSH is usually high.
Post-testicular: obstruction of the ducts; hormones are normal.
Cystic fibrosis: congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens gives obstructive azoospermia with low semen volume.
Varicocele impairs sperm production by raising scrotal temperature.

rows: Clear fluid in tunica vaginalis around testis
Smooth, testis hard to feel through fluid
Communicating type links to inguinal hernia
Look for an underlying testicular injury or tumor
Separate from testis, usually above it
Bag of worms, larger on standing
Infertility; new left one suggests renal cell carcinoma
Nocturnal erections kept in psychogenic cause

charts.title: Male infertility by level
rows: Kallmann syndrome, pituitary disease, anabolic steroids
Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, varicocele, mumps orchitis
Duct obstruction, absent vas deferens in cystic fibrosis

tricks.label: Point, Squeeze, and Shoot
tricks.text: Parasympathetic nerves cause erection (point), sympathetic nerves cause emission (squeeze), and somatic pudendal nerves cause ejaculation (shoot).

tricks.label: Light goes through water
tricks.text: Fluid that is clear (hydrocele, spermatocele) lets light through. Blood (hematocele), veins (varicocele), and solid tumors do not.

tricks.label: Left vein, long route
tricks.text: The left testicular vein empties into the left renal vein at a right angle, so pressure backs up easily. A renal tumor in that vein makes a new left varicocele.

highYield: Bag of worms that enlarges on standing and does not transilluminate: varicocele.
New left varicocele in an older man: think renal cell carcinoma in the left renal vein.
Transilluminating mass separate from and above the testis: spermatocele.
Transilluminating fluid around the testis in an infant: communicating hydrocele from a patent processus vaginalis.
Sudden severe testicular pain, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex: torsion.
Ischemic priapism in a patient with sickle cell disease; untreated it causes fibrosis and erectile dysfunction.
Normal nocturnal erections suggest psychogenic erectile dysfunction.
Cystic fibrosis causes infertility through absent vas deferens with normal testosterone.
pitfalls: Hydrocele surrounds the testis; spermatocele sits beside or above it. Both transilluminate.
Hematocele and hydrocele are both in the tunica vaginalis; only blood blocks the light.
Torsion loses the cremasteric reflex; epididymitis keeps it.
Peyronie disease is a plaque in the tunica albuginea; priapism is a prolonged erection without a plaque.

dumps.p: Draw a testis with its epididymis, tunica vaginalis, and spermatic cord. Draw and label where a hydrocele, hematocele, spermatocele, and varicocele form, and write beside each whether it transilluminates.

Hematocele: blood in tunica vaginalis, does not transilluminate
Spermatocele: cyst of the epididymis, separate from testis, transilluminates
Varicocele: pampiniform plexus in the cord, does not transilluminate
Varicocele enlarges on standing
Left testicular vein drains to left renal vein
Communicating hydrocele comes from a patent processus vaginalis

dumps.p: Make a table of the five types of erectile dysfunction. For each, write how it causes the problem and give one example. Add the test that points to a psychogenic cause.
l: Erection requires parasympathetic input, nitric oxide, and cGMP
Vascular: atherosclerosis limits inflow
Neurogenic: diabetes, spinal cord injury, pelvic surgery
Endocrine: hypogonadism or hyperprolactinemia
Drug-induced: an example drug class
Psychogenic: nocturnal erections are preserved
ED can be an early sign of coronary artery disease

summary: This unit covers breast disease, from inflammation and fibrocystic change to benign tumors and carcinoma. Exam questions ask which lumps raise cancer risk, which benign lesions mimic cancer, and how the main carcinoma types look under the microscope.

points: Nonproliferative change: cysts, apocrine metaplasia, fibrosis; no added cancer risk.
Proliferative change without atypia (usual hyperplasia, sclerosing adenosis, papilloma): slightly raised risk, about 1.5 to 2 times.
Atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia: moderately raised risk, about 4 to 5 times.
Acute mastitis: Staphylococcus aureus enters through cracked nipples while breastfeeding; red, warm, painful breast, fever, possible abscess.
Periductal mastitis: in smokers; squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts and keratin plugs give a painful subareolar mass or abscess.
Mammary duct ectasia: dilated subareolar ducts with thick secretions and plasma cell-rich inflammation in older multiparous women.
Duct ectasia scarring pulls the nipple in, so it can mimic carcinoma.
Galactocele: milk-filled duct cyst during lactation or weaning; rupture causes local inflammation.
Traumatic fat necrosis: nonenzymatic fat necrosis after trauma or surgery with foamy macrophages, giant cells, and calcification.
Fat necrosis forms a firm mass that can look like carcinoma on exam and mammography.
Fibroadenoma: most common benign tumor in young women; small, firm, mobile; stroma and ducts both proliferate.
Fibroadenoma is estrogen sensitive and can grow in pregnancy.
Phyllodes tumor: older women; leaf-like projections of overgrown, hypercellular stroma; can recur or metastasize.
Intraductal papilloma: benign papillary growth in a large subareolar duct; common cause of bloody nipple discharge.
Risk: age, family history, atypical hyperplasia, and long estrogen exposure.
Estrogen exposure: early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, late first pregnancy, postmenopausal obesity (fat aromatase).
Most common site is the upper outer quadrant.
DCIS: malignant cells confined by basement membrane; microcalcifications on mammography; comedo type has central necrosis.
Invasive ductal carcinoma: most common type; firm stellate mass with desmoplastic stroma.
Lobular carcinoma: E-cadherin (CDH1) loss makes cells discohesive; they invade in single-file lines; often bilateral and multifocal.
Paget disease: eczematous nipple from large Paget cells with clear cytoplasm in the epidermis; nearly always an underlying ductal carcinoma.
Inflammatory carcinoma: tumor emboli in dermal lymphatics cause erythema, edema, and peau d'orange.
Gynecomastia: benign ductal and stromal growth from a raised estrogen to androgen ratio; often bilateral and centered under the areola.
Causes: puberty, older age, cirrhosis, Klinefelter syndrome, some drugs.
Male breast carcinoma: linked to BRCA2 mutation and Klinefelter syndrome; firm, often one-sided mass.

tricks.label: Lobular loses its glue
tricks.text: E-cadherin holds cells together. Lobular carcinoma loses it, so cells drift apart and march in single file.

tricks.label: Fibroadenoma is the breast mouse
tricks.text: A small, smooth, very mobile lump in a young woman slips away under the fingers. That mobility is the classic fibroadenoma sign.

tricks.label: Count the estrogen years
tricks.text: Early menarche, late menopause, no pregnancies, late first pregnancy, and postmenopausal fat all add estrogen exposure, and each raises breast cancer risk.

highYield: Nonproliferative fibrocystic change carries no added cancer risk; atypical hyperplasia raises it about 4 to 5 times.
Breastfeeding woman with a red, painful breast and fever: Staphylococcus aureus mastitis.
Smoker with a painful subareolar mass: periductal mastitis from squamous metaplasia.
Bloody nipple discharge with a small subareolar lesion: intraductal papilloma.
Microcalcifications on mammography: DCIS; comedo type has central necrosis.
E-cadherin loss and single-file cells: invasive lobular carcinoma.
Eczematous nipple: Paget disease, which signals an underlying carcinoma.
Peau d'orange: inflammatory carcinoma with tumor in dermal lymphatics.
pitfalls: Fat necrosis and duct ectasia can look like cancer (mass, calcification, nipple retraction) but carry no added risk.
Phyllodes tumor is a stromal tumor of older women; do not call a large, fast-growing lump in a 50-year-old a fibroadenoma.
Inflammatory carcinoma looks infected but usually has no fever and occurs outside lactation.
Paget disease of the breast nearly always has an underlying carcinoma; vulvar Paget disease usually does not.

Proliferative without atypia: usual hyperplasia, sclerosing adenosis, papilloma
Proliferative without atypia raises risk about 1.5 to 2 times
Atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia raises risk about 4 to 5 times
DCIS is confined by the basement membrane
Invasive carcinoma has crossed the basement membrane
Fat necrosis and duct ectasia sit at the bottom despite mimicking cancer

summary: This unit covers the two common benign prostate problems: benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostatitis. Exam questions test where BPH grows and why that causes urinary symptoms, and which organism and time course fit each type of prostatitis.

points: Nodular hyperplasia of both glands and stroma in older men.
Grows in the transition (periurethral) zone, which wraps around the urethra.
Driven by DHT, made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase type 2 in stromal cells.
BPH is not a precursor of prostate carcinoma; carcinoma arises mostly in the peripheral zone.
PSA can be mildly raised in BPH.
Obstruction: hesitancy, weak stream, intermittent flow, incomplete emptying, dribbling.
Irritation from the straining bladder: frequency, urgency, nocturia.
Bladder wall hypertrophy and trabeculation, sometimes diverticula.
Urinary retention; stagnant urine favors infection and bladder stones.
Back pressure causes bilateral hydronephrosis and can cause postrenal kidney injury.
Older men: E. coli and other gram-negative rods, usually from infected urine refluxing into prostatic ducts.
Younger sexually active men: C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae.
Can follow catheterization or prostate procedures.
Fever, chills, dysuria, frequency, perineal or low back pain.
Rectal exam: tender, warm, swollen, boggy prostate.
Chronic bacterial: recurrent urinary tract infections with the same organism, because the prostate acts as a reservoir.
Often few systemic symptoms; low back pain, dysuria, perineal discomfort between episodes.
Chronic nonbacterial (chronic pelvic pain syndrome): months of pelvic pain with no bacteria on culture.
Chronic nonbacterial is the most common form of prostatitis.

tricks.label: Transition zone squeezes the tube
tricks.text: BPH grows in the zone wrapped around the urethra, so it causes obstruction early. Cancer grows in the outer peripheral zone, so it is felt on rectal exam before it causes symptoms.

tricks.label: Age picks the bug
tricks.text: Under about 35 and sexually active: think chlamydia and gonorrhea. Older man: think E. coli from the urine. The same rule works for epididymitis.

highYield: BPH is DHT-driven hyperplasia of the transition zone and is not premalignant.
Older man with hesitancy, weak stream, and nocturia: BPH.
BPH complications: retention, bladder hypertrophy, UTI, stones, bilateral hydronephrosis.
Fever, dysuria, and a tender boggy prostate in an older man: acute prostatitis from E. coli.
Recurrent UTIs with the same organism in a man: chronic bacterial prostatitis.
Chronic pelvic pain with negative cultures: chronic nonbacterial prostatitis.
pitfalls: BPH and carcinoma can coexist, but BPH does not turn into carcinoma.
A raised PSA does not by itself separate BPH from cancer; prostatitis can raise it too.
Chronic bacterial prostatitis is defined by the same organism coming back; chronic nonbacterial has no organism at all.
